# Systems and Hardware {#sec-appendix-systems}

This appendix provides a first-principles reference for the embedded systems, digital hardware architectures, and electrical dynamics that govern physical machine learning deployments. This reference distills the low-level interactions between software execution, interconnect contention, power delivery, and electro-mechanical dynamics, providing systems engineers and computer scientists with the quantitative tools necessary to achieve microsecond predictability and ensure hardware-level safety closure.

## How to Use This Appendix

Consult this appendix when diagnosing physical systems bottlenecks, timing jitter, electrical rail instability, or hardware interface boundaries across chapters in this book:

## Real-Time Timers, Watchdogs, and Schedulability {#sec-appendix-systems-timers}

In embedded real-time systems, temporal predictability is as vital as computational correctness. A late control action is not merely degraded; on physical hardware, it is incorrect and potentially destructive.

### Real-time task schedulability and response time analysis

A periodic real-time task $\tau_i$ is characterized by its worst-case execution time (WCET) $C_i$, relative deadline $D_i$, and period $T_i$.\index{Real-time systems!worst-case execution time} Under static-priority preemptive scheduling (such as Rate-Monotonic Scheduling [@liu1973scheduling]), schedulability across a set of tasks ordered by decreasing priority ($i = 1, \dots, n$) is verified by computing the worst-case **Response Time** $R_i$:
$$ R_i = C_i + B_i + I_i \le D_i $$
where $B_i$ is the maximum blocking duration induced by lower-priority tasks accessing shared resources, and $I_i$ is the interference from higher-priority tasks. The response time is computed via the fixed-point recurrence:
$$ R_i^{(k+1)} = C_i + B_i + \sum_{j \in hp(i)} \left\lceil \frac{R_i^{(k)}}{T_j} \right\rceil C_j $$
starting with $R_i^{(0)} = C_i$. Convergence occurs when $R_i^{(k+1)} = R_i^{(k)}$. If $R_i \le D_i$ for all tasks, the task set is deterministically schedulable under worst-case processor load.

### Hardware watchdogs and non-maskable interrupts

To enforce temporal deadlines at the silicon level, embedded architectures deploy **Hardware Watchdog Timers**.\index{Watchdog timer!hardware downcounter} A watchdog is an independent countdown register clocked by an isolated, low-frequency crystal oscillator.

The timer is initialized to a threshold value $W_{\text{init}}$. Software execution threads must periodically refresh (or "kick") the register before the count reaches zero. If $W(t)$ represents the register count at physical time $t$, and software executes a refresh at epoch $t_k$, the register resets:[^fn-sys-watchdog-reset]
$$ W(t_k) = W_{\text{init}} $$
If the processor hangs, deadlocks on a mutex, or exceeds its execution budget such that $W(t) \le 0$, the watchdog hardware underflows. This underflow immediately trips an external Non-Maskable Interrupt (NMI) or asserts a hardware reset line to the microcontroller, forcing the system into a safe fallback state within clock cycles.

[^fn-sys-watchdog-reset]: **Hardware Watchdog Down-Counters**\index{Watchdog timer!hardware downcounter}: Dedicated hardware watchdogs run on independent low-frequency crystal oscillators decoupled from main CPU core clocks. Software tasks must periodically refresh the down-counter before it underflows to prevent triggering a non-maskable interrupt or hard platform reset. Missing a watchdog refresh immediately disengages power inverter stages, preventing run-away actuator motion during operating system kernel panics.

## Inverter Timers and Power Electronics Gate Drive {#sec-appendix-systems-inverters}

Actuator motor drives employ three-phase half-bridge inverters to convert DC bus voltage into alternating stator currents.

### Microcontroller timer dead-time insertion

Each inverter phase comprises a high-side power MOSFET (or IGBT) and a low-side power MOSFET connected across the DC supply rail $V_{\text{bus}}$. Microcontroller timer peripherals generate complementary pulse-width-modulated (PWM) drive signals with hardware-enforced **dead-time insertion** $t_{\text{dead}}$:\index{Pulse-width modulation!dead-time insertion}
$$ t_{\text{dead}} \ge t_{\text{off, max}} + t_{\text{prop, skew}} - t_{\text{on, min}} $$
where $t_{\text{off, max}}$ is the maximum turn-off time of the power switch, $t_{\text{on, min}}$ is the minimum turn-on time, and $t_{\text{prop, skew}}$ is the propagation delay mismatch across gate drivers.[^fn-sys-pwm-deadtime]

Dead-time ensures that the high-side switch is fully non-conducting before the low-side switch begins conduction. If complementary switches conduct simultaneously—a catastrophic condition termed **shoot-through**—the DC rail is shorted directly to ground, drawing thousands of amperes per microsecond and destroying inverter silicon.

[^fn-sys-pwm-deadtime]: **Inverter Dead-Time Insertion**\index{Pulse-width modulation!dead-time insertion}: Microcontroller timer peripherals insert hardware dead-time between complementary gate drive outputs to compensate for finite power MOSFET turn-off delays. Failing to enforce dead-time permits both high-side and low-side switches in a half-bridge inverter to conduct simultaneously, causing a low-impedance shoot-through short circuit across the DC bus. Shoot-through events draw hundreds of amperes within nanoseconds, destroying inverter silicon and blowing primary battery protection fuses.

## Inductive Voltage Droop and Gate Delay Stretch {#sec-appendix-systems-droop}

When deep neural network accelerators (such as systolic array matrix engines) transition from idle to full execution, current draw increases by tens of amperes within nanoseconds.

### Power delivery network impedance and rail droop

Every power delivery network (PDN) exhibits finite parasitic loop inductance $L_{\text{PDN}}$ and equivalent series resistance $R_{\text{PDN}}$ across PCB traces, package balls, and bond wires. When accelerator execution triggers a transient current step $\Delta I$ with rise time $t_r$ (giving current slew rate $dI/dt \approx \Delta I / t_r$), Faraday's law of induction dictates an instantaneous voltage collapse $\Delta V_{\text{droop}}$:\index{Inductive voltage droop!power delivery network}
$$ \Delta V_{\text{droop}} = L_{\text{PDN}} \frac{dI}{dt} + \Delta I \cdot R_{\text{PDN}} $$
If supply voltage $V(t) = V_{\text{nom}} - \Delta V_{\text{droop}}$ sags below the minimum operating voltage $V_{\min}$, digital logic experiences severe timing degradation.

### Digital logic gate delay and the alpha-power law

In sub-micron CMOS silicon, logic gate propagation delay $t_{\text{prop}}$ is governed by the Sakurai-Newton **alpha-power law**:[^fn-sys-sakurai-droop]
$$ t_{\text{prop}}(V) \propto \frac{C_L \cdot V}{(V - V_{\text{th}})^\alpha} $$
where $C_L$ is the gate load capacitance, $V_{\text{th}}$ is the transistor threshold voltage, and $\alpha \in [1.2, 1.5]$ is the velocity saturation index (contrasting with $\alpha = 2.0$ in long-channel theory).

When rail voltage droops from $V_{\text{nom}}$ to $V_{\text{droop}}$, propagation delay stretches according to:
$$ \frac{t_{\text{prop}}(V_{\text{droop}})}{t_{\text{prop}}(V_{\text{nom}})} = \frac{V_{\text{droop}}}{V_{\text{nom}}} \left( \frac{V_{\text{nom}} - V_{\text{th}}}{V_{\text{droop}} - V_{\text{th}}} \right)^\alpha $$
In a synchronous digital pipeline with clock period $T_{\text{clk}}$, setup time $t_{\text{setup}}$, and clock skew $t_{\text{skew}}$, timing closure requires:
$$ t_{\text{prop}} + t_{\text{setup}} + t_{\text{skew}} \le T_{\text{clk}} $$
Stretching $t_{\text{prop}}$ causes setup slack to become negative, corrupting state registers or triggering supervisory brownout resets. On-package deep-trench decoupling capacitors (DTCs) mitigate this collapse by supplying high-frequency charge locally.

[^fn-sys-sakurai-droop]: **Sakurai-Newton Delay Modeling**\index{Gate delay!Sakurai-Newton model}: Takayasu Sakurai and A. Richard Newton formalized the alpha-power law in 1990 to capture carrier velocity saturation in sub-micron CMOS transistors. Supply voltage droop lengthens gate propagation delay nonlinearly, reducing digital setup slack across synchronous clock domains. Severe rail collapse violates flip-flop setup times, corrupting pipeline registers and triggering catastrophic processor brownout resets.

## DRAM Contention and Interconnect Arbitration {#sec-appendix-systems-dram}

In shared-memory multi-core system-on-chip (SoC) platforms, direct memory access (DMA) transfers and vision prefetching compete with real-time safety monitors for memory controller command queues and physical DRAM banks.

### DRAM bank organization and conflict latency

A DRAM chip is structured into multiple independent banks, each possessing a single row buffer. Accessing storage cells requires three sequential operations:\index{Memory contention!DRAM bank conflicts}

1. **Row activate** ($t_{\text{RCD}}$): Loads a row of storage cells into the bank's row buffer.
2. **Column access** ($t_{\text{CAS}}$): Reads or writes data from the open row buffer onto the data bus.
3. **Row precharge** ($t_{\text{RP}}$): Restores charge to storage capacitors and closes the active row.

When consecutive memory operations target different rows within the same physical bank (a *bank conflict* or *row-buffer miss*), the memory controller must precharge the active row and activate the requested row before column access can proceed, adding an access penalty of $t_{\text{RP}} + t_{\text{RCD}}$ ($28\text{--}40\text{ ns}$).[^fn-sys-dram-conflicts]

[^fn-sys-dram-conflicts]: **DRAM Bank-Conflict Penalties**\index{Memory contention!DRAM bank conflicts}: Accessing distinct rows within the same physical DRAM bank forces the memory controller to execute sequential precharge and activate cycles before reading columns. High-bandwidth direct memory access from video streaming engines can repeatedly stall real-time CPU safety threads seeking access to the same bank. Without hardware memory partitioning, this unmodeled bank contention inflates worst-case execution times by tens of microseconds, breaching hard real-time deadlines.

### Interconnect crossbars and burst contention

On-chip interconnect crossbars (such as AMBA AXI) schedule memory traffic in packet-atomic bursts. If a non-preemptive burst of size $B_{\text{burst}}$ (bytes) is in flight across a shared memory bus with bandwidth $\text{BW}_{\text{bus}}$ (bytes per second), an incoming real-time safety read waits for the in-flight burst duration:
$$ t_{\text{burst}} = \frac{B_{\text{burst}}}{\text{BW}_{\text{bus}}} $$
In the worst case where $K$ competing transactions are queued ahead of the real-time request and each induces a bank conflict, total queuing latency expands to:
$$ t_{\text{queue}} = \sum_{k=1}^K \frac{B_k}{\text{BW}_{\text{bus}}} + K (t_{\text{RP}} + t_{\text{RCD}}) + t_{\text{CAS}} $$
This queuing latency demonstrates why real-time safety critical state must be pinned in SRAM-based Tightly-Coupled Memory (TCM) rather than shared DDR channels.

## Clock Synchronization and Network Timestamps {#sec-appendix-systems-ptp}

Distributed multi-sensor perception pipelines require precise microsecond time synchronization across network nodes.

### Precision time protocol message exchange

The IEEE 1588 Precision Time Protocol (PTP) synchronizes a Slave clock ($S$) to a Master clock ($M$) by exchanging four physical timestamps across the communication link:\index{Precision Time Protocol!clock synchronization}

1. $t_1$: Master transmits a *Sync* frame, recording its local transmission timestamp.
2. $t_2$: Slave receives the *Sync* frame, recording its local arrival timestamp.
3. $t_3$: Slave transmits a *Delay_Req* frame, recording its local transmission timestamp.
4. $t_4$: Master receives the *Delay_Req* frame, recording its local arrival timestamp.

Assuming symmetric forward and reverse network propagation delay ($D_{M \to S} = D_{S \to M} = D$), the time relationships satisfy:
$$ t_2 = t_1 + O + D $$
$$ t_4 = t_3 - O + D $$
where $O$ is the clock offset between Slave and Master. Solving this system yields the exact clock offset:
$$ O = \frac{(t_2 - t_1) - (t_4 - t_3)}{2} $$
The one-way network propagation delay is:
$$ D = \frac{(t_2 - t_1) + (t_4 - t_3)}{2} $$
The slave corrects its local clock by subtracting offset $O$.

### Physical layer hardware timestamping

In software-based network implementations, timestamps are recorded inside operating system interrupt handlers, introducing unpredictable queuing and scheduling jitter ($10\text{--}100\text{ }\mu\text{s}$).

Under PTP hardware timestamping, timestamps $t_1, t_2, t_3, t_4$ are captured directly at the Ethernet physical transceiver (PHY) or Media Access Control (MAC) boundary as the start-of-frame delimiter passes the physical wire.[^fn-sys-ptp-timestamps] Bypassing operating system protocol stacks eliminates software jitter, providing sub-microsecond synchronization ($< 100\text{ ns}$) across distributed sensors.

[^fn-sys-ptp-timestamps]: **PHY-Layer Timestamping**\index{Precision Time Protocol!hardware timestamping}: IEEE 1588 Precision Time Protocol captures frame transmission and arrival timestamps directly at the physical Ethernet PHY transceiver. By recording timestamps at the physical line boundary, PTP eliminates the variable software queuing and interrupt dispatch jitter inherent in host operating system stacks. Sub-microsecond clock synchronization guarantees that distributed sensor measurements are referenced to a common temporal epoch before fusion filtering.

## Heterogeneous SoC Mailboxes and Memory Barriers {#sec-appendix-systems-ipc}

Modern robotics architectures deploy asymmetric multiprocessing (AMP) SoCs, coupling high-performance application processors (e.g., ARM Cortex-A running Linux) with real-time microcontrollers (e.g., ARM Cortex-M running bare-metal firmware).

### Remote processor messaging over shared SRAM

Inter-core communication utilizes statically allocated on-chip shared SRAM buffers synchronized via the Remote Processor Messaging (RPMSG) framework:\index{Inter-core communication!RPMSG framework}

1. Core A writes a message payload to a fixed buffer in shared SRAM.
2. Core A executes a hardware memory barrier to commit writes to physical memory.
3. Core A triggers an inter-processor interrupt (IPI) by writing to Core B's hardware mailbox register.
4. Core B services the interrupt, reads the buffer descriptor, and processes the payload.

### CPU pipeline reordering and memory fences

Modern out-of-order CPU pipelines and multi-level cache hierarchies speculatively reorder loads and stores to maximize execution throughput. In shared-memory IPC, this reordering can produce race conditions:\index{Memory barrier!instruction ordering}
```c
// Core A (Application Processor)
shared_buffer->target_torque = 15.0f; // Store 1: Payload
mailbox_doorbell = 1;                 // Store 2: Interrupt trigger
```
If the CPU or interconnect reorders Store 2 ahead of Store 1, Core B receives the interrupt before the new torque setpoint is committed to physical memory, reading stale or invalid data.

A **Memory Barrier** (or memory fence) enforces a strict happens-before ordering constraint:[^fn-sys-memory-barriers]
```c
shared_buffer->target_torque = 15.0f;
__asm__ volatile("dmb ish" ::: "memory"); // Data Memory Barrier
mailbox_doorbell = 1;
```
The data memory barrier (`DMB`) guarantees that all memory stores prior to the barrier are globally visible to all system cores and DMA masters before subsequent stores execute, ensuring data integrity across privilege boundaries.

[^fn-sys-memory-barriers]: **Hardware Memory Barriers**\index{Memory barrier!instruction ordering}: Modern out-of-order processors and write-combining memory controllers speculatively reorder loads and stores to maximize pipeline throughput. In inter-processor shared memory queues, stores to payload buffers must be globally visible across all cores before the signaling mailbox register is written. Omitting a data memory barrier permits receiving cores to process stale or corrupted payload data, commanding hazardous physical setpoints.

## Actuator Electrical and Thermal Dynamics {#sec-appendix-systems-actuators}

Actuators convert electrical energy into mechanical work through electromagnetic lorentz forces, subject to coupled electrical and thermal constraints.

### Stator electrical rise time

A brushless DC (BLDC) motor phase winding exhibits phase resistance $R_{\text{phase}}$ and phase inductance $L_{\text{phase}}$. Applying terminal voltage $V_{\text{terminal}}$ against back-electromotive force $e_{\text{bemf}} = K_e \omega_m$ yields the first-order stator current ODE:\index{Actuator!electrical rise time}
$$ L_{\text{phase}} \frac{dI(t)}{dt} + R_{\text{phase}} I(t) = V_{\text{terminal}} - K_e \omega_m $$
For a voltage step applied from rest ($\omega_m = 0$), phase current rises exponentially:
$$ I(t) = \frac{V_{\text{terminal}}}{R_{\text{phase}}} \left( 1 - e^{-t / \tau_e} \right), \quad \tau_e = \frac{L_{\text{phase}}}{R_{\text{phase}}} $$
where $\tau_e$ is the electrical time constant. Commanded torque $\tau_m = K_t I$ cannot rise faster than $\tau_e$, imposing a physical bandwidth limit on dynamic force generation.

### Lumped thermal networks and duty cycle

Current flowing through stator windings dissipates resistive Joule heat:
$$ P_{\text{loss}}(t) = I_{\text{rms}}^2(t) R_{\text{phase}}(T) $$
where copper resistance increases linearly with temperature:
$$ R_{\text{phase}}(T) = R_0 \left[ 1 + \alpha_{\text{Cu}} (T - T_0) \right] $$
with temperature coefficient $\alpha_{\text{Cu}} \approx 0.00393\text{ K}^{-1}$ for copper. In a single-node lumped thermal model with thermal resistance to ambient $\theta_{JA}$ (in $\text{K/W}$) and thermal heat capacity $C_{\text{th}}$ (in $\text{J/K}$), temperature rise $\Delta T(t) = T_{\text{winding}}(t) - T_{\text{ambient}}$ satisfies:[^fn-sys-motor-heating]
$$ C_{\text{th}} \frac{d\Delta T(t)}{dt} = P_{\text{loss}}(t) - \frac{\Delta T(t)}{\theta_{JA}} $$
Under constant power, temperature rises with thermal time constant $\tau_{\text{th}} = \theta_{JA} C_{\text{th}}$:
$$ \Delta T(t) = P_{\text{loss}} \theta_{JA} \left( 1 - e^{-t / \tau_{\text{th}}} \right) $$
Continuous torque capacity $\tau_{\text{cont}}$ is bounded by maximum allowable winding temperature $\Delta T_{\max}$:
$$ \tau_{\text{cont}} \le K_t \sqrt{\frac{\Delta T_{\max}}{\theta_{JA} R_{\text{phase}}}} $$
Peak torque $\tau_{\text{peak}} > \tau_{\text{cont}}$ is permitted only transiently, governed by the integral thermal capacity $\int_0^t I^2 dt \le I^2t_{\text{limit}}$.

[^fn-sys-motor-heating]: **Stator Thermal Time Constants**\index{Actuator!stator thermal dynamics}: Resistive Joule heating elevates motor phase winding temperatures during continuous high-torque maneuvers. Because copper electrical resistivity increases linearly with temperature, hot windings exhibit higher resistance, reducing torque output under terminal voltage saturation. Exceeding winding insulation temperature limits breaks down dielectric coatings, causing inter-turn short circuits and irreversible actuator destruction.

## DC Bus Power Distribution and Energy Absorption {#sec-appendix-systems-power}

A robotic platform's electrical power distribution network must supply acceleration surges and absorb regenerative braking energy across finite bus capacitance and harness impedance.

### Inductive droop and capacitive decoupling

When multiple actuators accelerate simultaneously, the aggregate current surge $\Delta I_{\text{bus}}$ draws from the battery through harness resistance $R_{\text{bus}}$ and inductance $L_{\text{bus}}$. Local bus capacitance $C_{\text{bus}}$ supplies transient charge. The peak voltage droop at the main DC-DC converter input is:
$$ \Delta V_{\text{droop}} \approx \Delta I_{\text{bus}} R_{\text{bus}} + L_{\text{bus}} \frac{dI_{\text{bus}}}{dt} + \frac{\Delta I_{\text{bus}} \Delta t}{2 C_{\text{bus}}} $$
If $\Delta V_{\text{droop}}$ drops the bus voltage below the under-voltage lockout (UVLO) threshold, the onboard power supply shuts down, resetting processors mid-motion.

### Regenerative braking surges and chopper sizing

During emergency deceleration, mechanical kinetic energy $E_k = \frac{1}{2} m v_0^2$ (linear) or $E_k = \frac{1}{2} J_{\text{load}} \dot{q}_0^2$ (rotational) is backdriven through motor inverters into the DC bus with regeneration efficiency $\eta_{\text{regen}} \approx 0.70\text{--}0.85$. If the battery management system (BMS) cannot accept rapid charge, the energy dumps into local DC bus capacitance $C_{\text{bus}}$, driving bus voltage upward:\index{Regenerative braking!chopper resistor}
$$ \Delta E_C = \frac{1}{2} C_{\text{bus}} \left( V_{\text{final}}^2 - V_{\text{initial}}^2 \right) = \eta_{\text{regen}} E_k $$
$$ V_{\text{final}} = \sqrt{ V_{\text{initial}}^2 + \frac{2 \eta_{\text{regen}} E_k}{C_{\text{bus}}} } $$
To prevent $V_{\text{final}}$ from exceeding the breakdown voltage rating of inverter MOSFETs ($V_{\max}$), an active **brake chopper** circuit shunts current through a power resistor $R_{\text{brake}}$ when $V_{\text{bus}} \ge V_{\text{clamp}}$:[^fn-sys-brake-chopper]
$$ R_{\text{brake}} \le \frac{V_{\text{clamp}}^2}{P_{\text{regen, peak}}} $$
$$ P_{\text{regen, peak}} \approx \eta_{\text{regen}} \cdot \tau_{\text{brake}} \cdot \omega_{\max} $$

[^fn-sys-brake-chopper]: **Dynamic Braking Choppers**\index{Regenerative braking!chopper resistor}: During rapid deceleration, backdriven kinetic energy returns to the DC power distribution bus via motor phase regeneration. When energy cannot be absorbed by the battery, bus capacitance charges rapidly, elevating voltage toward semiconductor breakdown thresholds. An active brake chopper shunts excess regenerative current through an external power resistor, dissipating kinetic energy as heat and preserving power electronics.

## Real-Time Fieldbuses and Lock-Free Synchronization {#sec-appendix-systems-fieldbus}

Coordinating distributed motor drives and compute nodes requires deterministic serialization protocols and lock-free memory exchange.

### Fieldbus serialization and schedulability

On a shared serial bus (such as CAN-FD or RS-485), $N_{\text{axes}}$ motor drives transmit telemetry and receive setpoints cyclically. For payload size $B_{\text{frame}}$ (bits) and transmission bitrate $R_{\text{baud}}$ (bps), transmission duration is $t_{\text{tx}} = B_{\text{frame}} / R_{\text{baud}}$.\index{Fieldbus!CAN-FD arbitration}

Under Controller Area Network (CAN-FD), nodes arbitrate via non-destructive bitwise arbitration. Total nominal cycle time across all axes is:
$$ T_{\text{bus}} = \sum_{i=1}^{N_{\text{axes}}} \left( \frac{B_{\text{payload}, i} + B_{\text{overhead}}}{R_{\text{data}}} + t_{\text{prop}} \right) $$
Under high bus utilization ($\rho = T_{\text{bus}} / T_{\text{target}} > 0.70$), collision retries increase nonlinearly, causing priority inversion and high message jitter.

In contrast, **EtherCAT** uses on-the-fly telegram processing: an Ethernet frame traverses an open ring topology through dedicated hardware controllers (application-specific integrated circuit [ASIC] or field-programmable gate array [FPGA]).\index{Fieldbus!EtherCAT on-the-fly} Slaves read and insert data directly within passing Ethernet frames with fixed forwarding latency $t_{\text{forward}} \approx 1\text{ }\mu\text{s}$ per node. Total cycle time is deterministic:
$$ T_{\text{EtherCAT}} = \frac{B_{\text{Ethernet frame}}}{R_{\text{EtherCAT}}} + N_{\text{axes}} \cdot t_{\text{forward}} + \frac{2 \cdot \text{Distance}}{v_{\text{prop}}} $$
enabling deterministic sub-millisecond cycle times ($<100\text{ }\mu\text{s}$) across dozens of synchronized axes.

### Lock-free seqlocks for multi-rate shared memory

When a single high-frequency writer (e.g., a $1\text{ kHz}$ IMU thread) updates multi-word kinematic state $\mathbf{x} \in \mathbb{R}^d$ read by low-frequency deliberative threads (e.g., a $20\text{ Hz}$ neural planner), mutexes introduce priority inversion.

A **sequence lock (seqlock)** provides lock-free synchronization using a monotonically incrementing integer sequence counter:\index{Concurrency!sequence locks}

1. **Writer Protocol**:
   - Increment sequence counter from even ($2k$) to odd ($2k+1$) using an atomic store with release semantics.
   - Insert a write memory barrier (`smp_wmb()`).
   - Update state data fields.
   - Insert a write memory barrier (`smp_wmb()`).
   - Increment sequence counter from odd ($2k+1$) to even ($2k+2$) with release semantics.
2. **Reader Protocol**:
   - Read sequence counter $S_1$ with acquire semantics. If $S_1$ is odd (writer active), spin or yield.
   - Insert a read memory barrier (`smp_rmb()`).
   - Copy state data fields locally.
   - Insert a read memory barrier (`smp_rmb()`).
   - Read sequence counter $S_2$ with acquire semantics.
   - If $S_1 \neq S_2$, data was torn during reading; retry loop.

Because writer duration is tiny ($t_{\text{write}} \approx 50\text{--}100\text{ ns}$ for 64 bytes of cache copy), reader collision probability is $< 0.01\%$, guaranteeing non-blocking real-time telemetry transfer.

## Camera Projective Geometry and Covariance Propagation {#sec-appendix-systems-vision}

Perception pipelines map continuous Euclidean 3D scenes onto discrete 2D camera photosite grids.

### Intrinsic projection matrix and radial distortion

Under the standard pinhole camera model, a 3D point $\mathbf{p}_c = [x_c, y_c, z_c]^\top$ in camera coordinates projects onto pixel coordinates $\mathbf{u} = [u, v]^\top$ via the intrinsic calibration matrix $\mathbf{K}$:[^fn-sys-pinhole-projection]
$$
\tilde{\mathbf{u}} = \begin{bmatrix} u \\ v \\ 1 \end{bmatrix} = \frac{1}{z_c} \mathbf{K} \mathbf{p}_c = \frac{1}{z_c} \begin{bmatrix} f_x & 0 & c_x \\ 0 & f_y & c_y \\ 0 & 0 & 1 \end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix} x_c \\ y_c \\ z_c \end{bmatrix}
$$
where $(f_x, f_y)$ are focal lengths in pixel units and $(c_x, c_y)$ is the principal point. Non-linear radial lens distortion is modeled by distortion coefficients $(k_1, k_2)$:
$$ r^2 = x_n^2 + y_n^2, \quad x_d = x_n (1 + k_1 r^2 + k_2 r^4), \quad y_d = y_n (1 + k_1 r^2 + k_2 r^4) $$
where $(x_n, y_n) = (x_c / z_c, y_c / z_c)$ are normalized image coordinates.

[^fn-sys-pinhole-projection]: **Pinhole Intrinsic Projection**\index{Camera model!pinhole projection}: The pinhole camera model projects 3D spatial points onto a discrete 2D sensor array via the intrinsic calibration matrix. Measurement noise on photosites unprojects into an anisotropic spatial error covariance that expands quadratically with true object distance. Uncalibrated intrinsic parameters distort perceived physical clearance, causing motion planners to generate collision-prone trajectory corridors.

### Metric unprojection and spatial covariance propagation

When unprojecting a 2D pixel observation $\mathbf{u}$ with measured depth $z$ into 3D camera coordinates, photosite measurement noise $\mathbf{\Sigma}_{\text{meas}} = \text{diag}(\sigma_u^2, \sigma_v^2, \sigma_z^2)$ propagates through the unprojection Jacobian $\mathbf{J}_{\text{unproj}}$:\index{Mathematics!covariance propagation}
$$
\mathbf{p}_c = \begin{bmatrix} (u - c_x) z / f_x \\ (v - c_y) z / f_y \\ z \end{bmatrix}, \quad \mathbf{\Sigma}_c = \mathbf{J}_{\text{unproj}} \mathbf{\Sigma}_{\text{meas}} \mathbf{J}_{\text{unproj}}^\top
$$
Transforming this 3D point into the robot body frame via rigid extrinsic transform $\mathbf{T}_{bc} = [\mathbf{R}_{bc}, \mathbf{p}_{bc}; \mathbf{0}^\top, 1]$ yields the spatial body covariance:
$$ \mathbf{\Sigma}_b = \mathbf{R}_{bc} \mathbf{\Sigma}_c \mathbf{R}_{bc}^\top + \mathbf{\Sigma}_{\text{ext}} $$
where $\mathbf{\Sigma}_{\text{ext}}$ represents structural mounting compliance and thermal calibration drift. Downstream safety filters evaluate the maximum eigenvalue $\lambda_{\max}(\mathbf{\Sigma}_b)$ to expand geometric collision-clearance buffers proportionally to sensor uncertainty.

## Kinematic Stopping Envelopes and Information Age Lag {#sec-appendix-systems-stopping}

Halting an embodied machine transporting mass $m$ at velocity $v_0$ requires balancing sensorimotor information freshness and mechanical braking deceleration.

### Sensorimotor information age and lag distance

The total end-to-end information age $\tau_{\text{info}}$ from initial physical photon arrival to mechanical torque application is the sum of pipeline latencies across all tiers:\index{Kinematic stopping distance!information age}
$$ \tau_{\text{info}} = t_{\text{sensor}} + t_{\text{compute}} + t_{\text{bus}} + t_{\text{actuator}} $$
where:

- $t_{\text{sensor}}$ is the physical exposure and frame readout interval.
- $t_{\text{compute}}$ is the DMA transfer, neural inference, and trajectory verification latency.
- $t_{\text{bus}}$ is the serial fieldbus transmission and arbitration delay.
- $t_{\text{actuator}}$ is the stator inductive current rise time ($\tau_e = L / R$) and mechanical brake engagement delay.

During this latency window $\tau_{\text{info}}$, the vehicle continues unbraked at speed $v_0$, traversing unbraked lag distance:
$$ d_{\text{lag}} = v_0 \cdot \tau_{\text{info}} $$

### Braking dynamics and friction limits

Once braking torque engages, maximum physical deceleration $a_{\text{brake}}$ is limited by the Coulomb friction coefficient $\mu$ between tire and floor, or by actuator torque ceilings:\index{Braking!friction limit}
$$ a_{\text{brake}} \le \mu g $$
The physical braking distance is:
$$ d_{\text{brake}} = \frac{v_0^2}{2 a_{\text{brake}}} \ge \frac{v_0^2}{2 \mu g} $$
The total kinematic stopping envelope $d_{\text{stop}}(v_0)$ is the sum of lag distance and braking distance:
$$ d_{\text{stop}}(v_0) = d_{\text{lag}} + d_{\text{brake}} = v_0 \tau_{\text{info}} + \frac{v_0^2}{2 \mu g} $$
Deterministic safety closure requires that this stopping envelope remain strictly within the measured clearance buffer $d_{\text{clear}}$:
$$ d_{\text{stop}}(v_0) \le d_{\text{clear}} $$

### Kinetic energy derating and friction collapse

If surface contamination (such as water, oil, or ice) causes friction to collapse from nominal $\mu_{\text{nom}}$ to degraded $\mu_{\text{fault}} \ll \mu_{\text{nom}}$, braking distance expands inversely with friction:\index{Velocity clamp!kinetic derating}
$$ \frac{d_{\text{brake}}(\mu_{\text{fault}})}{d_{\text{brake}}(\mu_{\text{nom}})} = \frac{\mu_{\text{nom}}}{\mu_{\text{fault}}} $$
When forward friction cannot be continuously monitored prior to braking, the system enforces safety by clamping maximum forward velocity $v_{\text{clamp}}$ in firmware. Solving $v_{\text{clamp}} \tau_{\text{info}} + \frac{v_{\text{clamp}}^2}{2 \mu_{\text{fault}} g} \le d_{\text{clear}}$ yields the certified velocity clamp:
$$ v_{\text{clamp}} = -\mu_{\text{fault}} g \tau_{\text{info}} + \sqrt{(\mu_{\text{fault}} g \tau_{\text{info}})^2 + 2 \mu_{\text{fault}} g d_{\text{clear}}} $$
By clamping forward speed to $v_{\text{clamp}}$, the physical stopping envelope is guaranteed to remain within clearance bounds even under catastrophic friction loss, establishing deterministic safety without continuous friction sensing.

## Further Reading

For a deeper foundational understanding of embedded architectures, real-time operating systems, and power electronics, consult the following authoritative references:

* **Computer Organization and Design: The Hardware/Software Interface** [@hennessy2019computer] provides the definitive treatment of processor architectures, cache hierarchies, and memory subsystem trade-offs.
* **Scheduling Algorithms for Multiprogramming in a Hard-Real-Time Environment** [@liu1973scheduling] establishes the mathematical foundations of rate-monotonic scheduling and real-time task schedulability.
* **Modern Operating Systems** by Andrew S. Tanenbaum and Herbert Bos provides comprehensive coverage of inter-process communication, lock-free synchronization, and memory management.
* **Real-Time Systems** by Jane W. S. Liu delivers the authoritative mathematical formulation of real-time scheduling algorithms, priority inversion, and response time analysis.
